manifest.name: dsh-model-router
manifest.description: Question-type-aware model routing for DeepSeek Harness: correctness first for research tasks, free models first for small talk

bundle.text:
# The config layer this package contributes: insert the router into the Loader tree.
# Applied automatically once a profile lists this package in dsh.profile.bundles.
- insert:
    - id: dsh-model-router
      name: dsh-model-router
      config:
        enabled: true

        # Off by default so the first enable is observable rather than silent:
        # with dryRun the router only logs what it WOULD pick and changes nothing.
        dryRun: false

        # Where an unclassifiable model or exhausted candidate pool lands.
        # The native DeepSeek route: always configured, no third-party gateway.
        fallback:
          provider: deepseek-account
          model: deepseek-flash

        # Research-type tasks are quality-first: cost only breaks ties.
        research:
          types:
            - learning_tutor
            - coding
            - math_reasoning
            - knowledge_qa
            - agentic_tools
          # Hard floor regardless of cost. null = take whatever scores highest.
          # This key was documented here and never read by the policy, so setting it
          # changed nothing at all. It is now enforced BEFORE the top rating is
          # taken. If a floor would empty the pool the router relaxes it and says so
          # in the reason, because a mistyped floor should not silence the turn.
          minScore: null

        # Small talk is efficiency-first: any model clearing the floor is
        # acceptable, and among those the free ones win.
        casual:
          types:
            - daily_chat
          minScore: 3
          preferFree: true

        # Everything else: near-best quality, then cheapest of those.
        # maxScoreDrop: 0 keeps ONLY the exact top score in contention, so a
        # lower-rated free model cannot displace a specialist that sits at the
        # top of the rating (e.g. Claude/GPT for writing).
        #
        # `translation` was listed here and has now been removed on purpose: 30 of
        # its 64 ratings are null and the matrix's own caveats say "do not route on
        # it". A configured policy for a column that is mostly missing means
        # translation turns almost always fall through to the fallback route.
        balanced:
          types:
            - writing_literature
            - long_context
          maxScoreDrop: 0

        # Types with no configured policy fall here and are ordered by price alone.
        # `translation` is the live example and it is deliberate: 32 of its ratings
        # are tier inference at `confidence: low`, and the matrix's own caveats say
        # not to route on that column — so price is the only honest tie-break left.
        # The floor stops "cheapest" from reaching a model rated 1 at everything.
        # Raising it will not improve translation quality; only real data will.
        defaultPolicy:
          minScore: 2

        # Specialty preference — the "brain vs executor" split. Among models tied
        # at the SAME top score, prefer these model-id substrings (in order)
        # before falling back to price.
        #
        # How the preference is applied changed. It used to be a lexicographic
        # override: on a tie the first matching brand won outright. It is now a
        # bounded bonus, `preferBonus / (1 + rank)`, so it can only reorder a
        # genuine tie — every one of the 446 ratings in the matrix is an integer on
        # a 1-5 scale, so no bonus below 1 can outrank a real one-point gap — and
        # the second-choice brand can no longer overtake the first on price.
        #
        # Two further corrections. It now matches the MODEL ID only, not the
        # provider name: a gateway called `claude-proxy` used to hand top
        # preference to every model it served. And it does not apply to a
        # candidate whose rating is explicitly `low`/`unknown` confidence: those
        # numbers are tier inference, not measurements, and letting a brand list
        # arbitrate between them is a decision dressed up as evidence. That case is
        # live today — `learning_tutor` has 31 models tied at its top rating and
        # every one of them is rated from inference, so this entry currently has no
        # effect on that type, which is the honest outcome.
        #
        # It applies to brain turns only (hard/moderate, plus the types that are
        # inherently reasoning work); trivial repetitive turns stay on the cheapest
        # qualifying model. A type omitted here keeps pure "price breaks ties".
        prefer:
          coding: ["claude", "gpt"]
          math_reasoning: ["gpt", "gemini", "claude"]
          knowledge_qa: ["claude", "gpt", "gemini", "grok"]
          learning_tutor: ["claude", "gpt", "gemini"]
          agentic_tools: ["claude", "gpt"]
          writing_literature: ["claude", "gpt"]
          long_context: ["claude", "gemini", "gpt"]

        # Bounded nudges applied on top of the recorded rating. Both are below 1 on
        # purpose: the rating scale is integers, so anything at or above 1 would let
        # a preference outrank a genuine quality gap. Set either to 0 to switch it
        # off. These must be numbers — a quoted "0.5" fails at mount rather than
        # being silently ignored at decision time.
        preferBonus: 0.5
        reasoningBonus: 0.25 # a probe-verified reasoning model, on reasoning-shaped types
        # A preference may only buy a BOUNDED premium. Two models rated equal are
        # equal, and without this the brand list is an open-ended cheque: at 37x the
        # price gap a flash model loses to Opus on a tie. Raise it to express brand
        # priority deliberately; set it to a huge number to make prefer absolute.
        preferPriceCap: 4

        # Context-window feasibility. The router used to read no window at all, so a
        # 200K conversation could be routed to a 128K model and silently truncated.
        # The window now comes from the provider's own `resolveModelInfo`, which is
        # the only authoritative value; the matrix is a per-provider opt-in below.
        # The token estimate is deliberately high: under-estimating loses the whole
        # turn to truncation, over-estimating only costs a more expensive route.
        respectContext: true
        contextHeadroom: 1.15 # reserve for the response on top of the estimate
        promptOverheadTokens: 8000 # system prompt + tool schemas, absent from messages
        # Falling back to the matrix window is ON by default: those values come from
        # vendor documentation and all 52 of them are plausible, and switching the
        # fallback off would leave the gate inert on any provider whose
        # resolveModelInfo does not answer. The matrix NEVER overrides a live value —
        # it only fills a gap. List a provider under `exclude` if you have checked
        # its window is overstated, since an overstated window admits a model that
        # truncates, and truncation loses the work rather than the money.
        contextWindowFallback:
          default: true
          exclude: []

        # The capability matrix is a snapshot of a market that moves weekly, and
        # nothing used to notice when it aged. Past this age the router warns at
        # boot and reports the age in /route. Rebuild with:
        #   node tools/probe-catalog.mjs && node tools/build-capabilities.mjs
        maxMatrixAgeDays: 45

        # Cooldowns. The provider-level entry is the important one: rate limits are
        # enforced per account or gateway, so several models sharing one key each
        # holding only a model-scoped cooldown just took turns hitting the same wall.
        # Consecutive failures at a provider double its window up to the cap, and
        # one completed turn resets the streak.
        cooldownMs: 120000
        providerCooldownMs: 60000
        maxCooldownMs: 600000
        # One flat window for an exhausted daily allowance (`quota`), which resets
        # on a schedule — escalating it walks the whole gateway out of service for
        # the rest of the day. A spent billing balance (`insufficient_quota`) is
        # NOT governed by this: that is permanent and takes maxCooldownMs instead.
        quotaTtlMs: 120000

        # Types forced to be treated as brain work regardless of difficulty, so a
        # configured `prefer` entry applies to them even on a trivial turn. EMPTY by
        # default: forcing it cost 33x on a six-character request ("优化下这段代码"
        # went to the most expensive coder), because difficulty cannot reliably tell
        # a one-line hard bug from a one-line easy one. Add a type only if you want
        # that trade, knowing the short turns pay for it.
        alwaysBrainTypes: []

        # Grok on this gateway cannot call tools, so it may never serve a turn
        # that executes a task. This list is the only place it is allowed.
        #
        # That is no longer enforced here by name. Whether a model can call tools
        # is settled by the capability record — its own probe reached Grok, forced
        # tool_choice, and got no tool call — so the tool gate excludes it on
        # measurement. What remains below is purely the deployment's own rule about
        # where Grok may serve at all, and `match` is configurable so the policy is
        # not welded to a provider name that may change.
        grok:
          enabled: true
          allowedTypes:
            - daily_chat
          # match: /^(grok|xai)\b|^grok[-_]/i

        # The per-session "工作 / 闲聊" mode. `work` keeps the type-based policy
        # above exactly as-is; `chat` steers the whole turn toward free models
        # (Space Bunny Free first), and lets a genuinely hard question escalate
        # to Grok for reasoning. The /mode command writes a durable map
        # (data/modes.json) AND a `model-router/mode` session event; `defaultMode`
        # is the value a session uses before it has ever been toggled. Routing
        # reads the map, never the session log, because resolving a live session
        # at route time can silently miss.
        defaultMode: work
        # Override where that map lives (the tests point it at a temp file).
        # stateFile: ./data/modes.json
        chat:
          # The free model chat mode prefers first (must be free in the matrix).
          preferred:
            id: space-bunny-free

        # After routing, write the chosen model back into the session's durable
        # model selection so the composer's model seat switches to it and the
        # user can see what actually served the turn. Disable if you prefer the
        # selection to stay untouched.
        reflectModel: true

        # Keep small talk short at the wire level (a hard bound, independent of
        # instruction following). null disables the cap.
        chitchatMaxTokens: 700

        # Tone control for small talk: contributes a system-prompt section that
        # appears ONLY on small-talk turns, so every other prompt stays
        # byte-identical. Note that a section which toggles turn to turn changes
        # the system-prompt prefix, which is what a prompt cache keys on —
        # disable this if cache reuse matters more than tone.
        chitchatStyle:
          enabled: true
          # directive: override the built-in wording entirely.

        # Auxiliary calls (session title, compaction) carry a purpose and keep
        # whatever model the harness chose; their output format is contractual.
        respectPurpose: true

        # Provider/model pairs routing must never override, as "provider/model".
        # Use this to protect a model pinned by configuration, e.g. a subagent's
        # agentOptions.provider/model.
        respectModels: []

        # Never route a request carrying an image to a text-only model.
        respectModalities: true

readme.text:
Question-type-aware model routing for DeepSeek Harness.

Instead of one model answering everything, the router classifies each turn and
re-dispatches it to the model that fits — correctness first for research work,
free models first for small talk.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/<you>/dsh-model-router.git
cp -r dsh-model-router ~/.dsh/plugins/
```

Then list `dsh-model-router` in `dsh.profile.bundles` in your profile's
`cordis.patch.yml`. The plugin contributes its own `config:` block — see
[cordis.patch.yml](cordis.patch.yml) for the annotated defaults.

**Start with `dryRun: true`.** The router then only logs what it *would* pick and
changes nothing, so you can watch it against your own catalogue before letting it
move real traffic.

| Task kind | Objective |
| --- | --- |
| `coding`, `math_reasoning`, `learning_tutor`, `knowledge_qa`, `agentic_tools` | **quality-first**: the highest-rated model wins outright; price only breaks ties among equally-rated candidates |
| `daily_chat` | **efficiency-first**: any model clearing the score floor is acceptable, and among those the free ones win |
| `writing_literature`, `translation`, `long_context` | near-best (within `maxScoreDrop` of the top), then cheapest |

- **Grok is barred from every turn that executes a task.** On the configured
  gateway it never receives tool schemas, so it may only serve the types listed
  under `grok.allowedTypes` (default: small talk) and never a turn carrying tool
  activity or an action request.
- **Unknown is not a guess.** A model with no capability record, or whose tool
  support is unknown on a tool-executing turn, is excluded; if nothing
  qualifies the request is routed to `fallback` — or left untouched when no
  fallback is configured and live.
- **Rate-limited routes cool down** instead of being retried every turn.
- **Auxiliary calls are never routed.** Session-title and compaction requests
  carry a `purpose` and keep the model the harness chose, because their output
  format is contractual. `respectPurpose: false` disables this.
- **Pinned models can be exempted.** `respectModels: ["provider/model"]` makes
  routing leave those requests alone — the escape hatch for a subagent whose
  model is pinned by `agentOptions`.

`maxTokens` bounds small-talk length at the wire level, but tone needs a prompt.
The plugin contributes one system-prompt section (`model-router:chitchat-style`)
that renders **only** on small-talk turns; on every other turn it renders empty
and is dropped, so those prompts are byte-identical to one assembled without
this plugin.

Turn correlation is exact rather than bookkeeping: the assembly hook's `scope`
is the Agent, and an Agent exposes `.session`, so the latest genuine user
message is read straight off the session (plugin-authored context and tool
results are skipped — they are user-role messages too).

⚠️ A section that toggles turn to turn changes the system-prompt prefix, which
is what a prompt cache keys on. Set `chitchatStyle.enabled: false` if cache
reuse matters more than tone.

Both keep working: the router swaps which model serves a stream and nothing
else. Spawning, the team task board, messaging, tool exposure and the
subagent/teammate model *selection* are all untouched.

Every `llm/stream` call is routed, including a child agent's own turns — so a
subagent doing code gets a coding model. A child's selection is inherited from
its parent (or pinned by `agentOptions`); use `respectModels` to protect a pin.

It hooks the `llm/stream` waterfall — the seam the harness documents as where
provider/model routing is replaced — and returns a **new request envelope**.
The incoming request is never mutated: loop-built requests are deep-frozen and
their content is a pure function of the session log.

Everything lives in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml` under this plugin's
`config:`. See [cordis.patch.yml](cordis.patch.yml) for the annotated defaults.

Useful switches:

- `dryRun: true` — log what it *would* pick and change nothing. Do this first.
- `enabled: false` — leave every request exactly as the caller built it.
- `chunk` limits: `chitchatMaxTokens` bounds small-talk output at the wire level.

A user-selected override steers the whole turn, independent of the task type:

- `work` (default) — the type-based policy above, unchanged.
- `chat` — free models first: **Space Bunny Free** is preferred, then the rest of
  the free pool; a genuinely hard question (not a tool-executing turn) may
  escalate to **Grok** for reasoning.

Mode is per-session. The composer's ⚡ 工作 / 闲聊 toggle (in the model-selector
row) writes it; `/mode` (or `/mode work|chat`) shows or sets it. Three sources
keep it reliable, in precedence order:

1. **`data/modes.json`** — the plugin's own map, written by `/mode` and read by
   the router on every turn. This is the source routing trusts, so a switch
   applies on the very next turn and survives a restart.
2. **the `model-router/mode` session event** — appended by `/mode` as the
   semantic record in the session log, and read back for a session whose mode
   predates the state file.
3. **`defaultMode`** — the value a session uses before it has ever been toggled.

`stateFile` overrides where that map lives (the tests point it at a temp file),
and `chat.preferred.id` names the free model chat mode prefers first.

The state file exists because reading the mode back out of the session log at
route time is not dependable: resolving the live session for a turn can miss, and
a miss is **silent** — the mode simply stays at its default even though the write
itself succeeded. Routing therefore never depends on that read.

When the router picks a different model, it writes that pick back into the
session's durable model selection, so the composer's model seat **switches to the
model that actually served the turn** — you can see what answered you.
`reflectModel: false` disables this and leaves the selection untouched.

`/route` prints the last decision: the classified kind, its confidence, whether
tools were required, the mode in effect, what the caller asked for, what was
chosen, and why.

`data/capabilities.json` is the capability matrix the policy reads: per model,
nine task ratings with their source URL and confidence, price, modality, and
measured facts (reachability, tool calling, time-to-first-token) from live
probing. `tools/` holds the probes that produced it; `tools/validate-profile.mjs`
checks a profile's provider section against the adapter's own schema.

Capability confidence is uneven by nature: vendor benchmark figures are `high`,
tier inference anchored on metadata is `low`, and unverifiable ids are `unknown`.
`translation` is almost entirely unmeasured and should not be routed on.

The matrix is a snapshot and ages; the router warns at boot past
`maxMatrixAgeDays`. To re-measure it against **your own** gateways, copy
`gateways.local.json.example` to `gateways.local.json` and list the endpoints you
want probed:

```json
[{ "route": "my-gateway", "base": "https://api.example.com/v1", "keyEnv": "MY_GATEWAY_API_KEY" }]
```

`keyEnv` names a key in `~/.dsh/.credentials.yaml`, so no credential is ever
written into this repository. Then `node tools/probe-catalog.mjs` and rebuild with
`node tools/build-capabilities.mjs`.

readme.section: What is deliberately not in this repository
readme.text:
The router writes and reads state that identifies *your* usage, and probing needs
to know *which* services you pay for. None of it is tracked:

| File | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `data/modes.json` | session ID → work/chat |
| `data/diagnostics.log` | every routing decision, timestamped |
| `data/probe-*.json`, `data/research-*.json` | raw gateway responses and catalogue dumps |
| `gateways.local.json` | your gateway endpoints and the credential each one uses |

readme.section: What is deliberately not in this repository
readme.text: All are covered by `.gitignore` and are created on demand at runtime.

```sh
node --test test/*.test.mjs
```

Roughly 100 tests: classifier behaviour, every policy rule above, and an
integration suite that mounts the real plugin into a real cordis context and
asserts actual dispatch decisions. Two `mode-e2e` cases covering restore-from-
session-log are currently red — they fail on the author's machine too and are
unrelated to routing.
